query: The (MnNiSi)0.62(FeCoGe)0.38 high-entropy alloy is a solid refrigeration working medium that exhibits a large caloric response under applied-field and pressure-field operation but has poor load-bearing integrity and tends to crack. What single intervention could increase its integrity while preserving caloric performance in these operating regimes? State one hypothesis specifying the intervention, its proposed mechanism, predicted integrity and caloric outcomes relative to the unchanged alloy, applicable field, pressure, temperature, and loading boundaries, supporting prior evidence, and a controlled experiment with explicit results that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Introducing 0.3–0.5 at% boron into (MnNiSi)0.62(FeCoGe)0.38 strengthens grain boundaries and reduces cracking while preserving its magnetocaloric and barocaloric effects under 0–2 T fields and up to ~1 GPa compressive loads at 280–320 K.
generation.material_initial_state: Undoped (MnNiSi)0.62(FeCoGe)0.38 alloy exhibiting large caloric response but low load-bearing integrity and a tendency to crack under applied magnetic and pressure fields.
generation.intervention: Minor boron addition (0.3–0.5 at%) via vacuum induction melting with controlled microalloying, followed by homogenization.
generation.conditions: Evaluate mechanical and caloric properties under magnetic fields up to 2 T or compressive stresses up to ~1 GPa, at temperatures of 280–320 K.
generation.structural_mediator: Segregation of boron to grain boundaries to enhance cohesion and inhibit crack initiation and propagation.
generation.mechanism: Boron-enriched grain boundaries improve fracture resistance by reducing intergranular embrittlement without disrupting the principal magnetocaloric and barocaloric phase transformations.
generation.predicted_outcome: Significantly increased fracture toughness and load-bearing capacity relative to the undoped alloy, with no more than ~10% reduction in caloric performance metrics under both magnetic and pressure fields.
generation.baseline: Pure (MnNiSi)0.62(FeCoGe)0.38 alloy with poor mechanical integrity and susceptibility to cracking during caloric operation.
generation.boundary: Operable up to 2 T and ~1 GPa at 280–320 K for refrigeration cycles where repeated mechanical or field loading is expected.
generation.uncertainty: Direct experimental data on boron doping in this alloy are limited; however, boron microalloying in analogous alloys has demonstrated effective grain-boundary strengthening without compromising functional properties.

falsification_experiment.design: Produce two batches of (MnNiSi)0.62(FeCoGe)0.38 samples: one undoped (control) and one with 0.3–0.5 at% boron. Perform vacuum induction melting and homogenization. Subject both sets to identical magnetic fields (0–2 T) and compressive loads (0–1 GPa) over 280–320 K, simulating typical refrigeration cycles.
measurements: 1) Fracture toughness and compressive strength, measured before and after cyclical loading.
2) Magnetocaloric effect and barocaloric effect, quantified by isothermal entropy changes at relevant fields and pressures.
3) Microstructural characterization (grain boundary inspection, crack propagation).
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If boron doping does not yield a measurable increase in fracture toughness or if it reduces overall caloric performance by more than 10%, the hypothesis is falsified.

FeCrNiCu based high entropy alloy matrix composites were fabricated with addition of Si and C by vacuum electromagnetic induction melting. The primary goal of this research was to analyze the reaction mechanism, microstructure, mechanical properties at room temperature and strengthening mechanism of the composites with addition of Si and C. The reaction mechanism of powders containing (Si, Ni and C) was analyzed, only one reaction occurred (i.e., Si + C → SiC) and its activation energy is 1302.8 kJ/mol. The new composites consist of a face centered cubic (FCC) structured matrix reinforced by submicron sized SiC particles. The addition of Si and C enhances the hardness from 351.4 HV to 626.4 HV and the tensile strength from 565.5 MPa to 846.0 MPa, accompanied by a slight decrease in the plasticity. The main strengthening mechanisms of SiC/FeCrNiCu composites were discussed based on dislocation strengthening, load bearing effect, Orowan mechanism and solid solution hardening, whose contributions to the tensile strength increase are 58.6%, 6.3%, 14.3% and 20.8%, respectively.

The in-situ composites containing of FeCrNiCu high entropy alloy matrix and SiC particles were designed and prepared by vacuum electromagnetic induction melting. The reaction process of the Si-Ni-C system consists of one step; i.e., Si reacting with C to form SiC particles as reinforcement phase. The activation energy of the reaction was found to be 1302.8 kJ/mol. The matrix of the as-sintered composites is mainly composed of Cu-rich phase and Cu-poor phase. The mechanical properties of the composites are significantly improved by the presence of SiC reinforcement phase. The hardness of SC10 is 78.3% higher than that of the matrix. The tensile strength of the composite is 846.0 MPa, which is 49.6% greater than that of the matrix. The multiple strengthening mechanisms were identified; namely, dislocation strengthening, load bearing effect, Orowan mechanism and solid solution strengthening. Among them the major contribution is from dislocation strengthening, which raised the tensile strength of the matrix by 58.6%.

chosen.why: We propose introducing a small fraction of boron (on the order of 0.3–0.5 at%) into the (MnNiSi)0.62(FeCoGe)0.38 alloy to foster grain-boundary strengthening and reduce crack propagation during applied magnetic and pressure fields. Boron atoms tend to segregate to grain boundaries, promoting cohesion and reducing the likelihood of brittle failure, while preserving the main magneto- and barocaloric mechanisms because the primary phase constitution remains largely unchanged. This approach is supported by prior evidence in related alloys, where microalloying with boron significantly enhanced mechanical strength without compromising functional performance. To test the hypothesis, a controlled experiment would compare the fracture toughness, tensile/compressive strength, and caloric properties (magnetocaloric under up to 2 T and barocaloric under up to ~1 GPa) of the boron-doped alloy relative to the undoped composition at 280–320 K. Failure to observe a meaningful increase in mechanical integrity or a severe drop (>10%) in caloric capacity would falsify the hypothesis.
